segments.text: You're gripping a shield, screaming down a hillside toward a shieldwall, and two long curved horns jut off your helmet, cutting the air on either side of your head. The horns catch the firelight. They look terrifying. They look exactly like every painting, every movie poster, every Halloween costume you've ever seen of a Viking. This is the image burned into your head.
A single wrong picture like this can quietly rewrite an entire culture's history in our heads.
So did any Viking ever actually strap on horns before walking into battle?

Here's the belief almost everyone carries around without question: Viking raiders wore horned helmets into combat, the horns curving up from the sides like a bull's. It feels obvious. It's on flags, beer labels, football helmets. But archaeologists digging across Scandinavia for over a century have found remarkably few actual Viking-age helmets at all. Total confirmed helmets from the entire Viking Age, roughly 793 to 1066, that survive with enough of the skull intact to study? You can count them on one hand.

The best-preserved one is the Gjermundbu helmet, dug out of a burial mound in Norway in 1943, dated to around the year 970. It has a rounded iron cap, a spectacled guard curving over the eyes and nose, and absolutely nothing where horns would attach. No sockets. No rivet holes shaped for anything curved. Just a plain iron dome built to deflect a sword, not to look dramatic.

Why trust one helmet? Because it isn't alone. Fragments from Tjele in Denmark and a handful of other sites all show the same story: plain iron, sometimes mail hanging to protect the neck, occasionally a nose guard. Historian Roberta Frank, who spent years tracing this myth through Old Norse literature, found zero contemporary written descriptions of horned battle helmets either. Not one saga. Not one carving from the era mentions warriors fighting in horns.

So where do actual horned helmets in museums come from, if not the Viking Age? Rewind about two thousand years before the first Viking ship ever launched. In 1942, workers draining a bog near Veksø in Denmark pulled up two bronze helmets, each fitted with long, gently curving horns tipped with little round discs. They're called the Veksø helmets, and they've been dated to roughly 900 to 1100 BCE, the Nordic Bronze Age.

These weren't armor. The bronze is thin, decorative, almost delicate. They were likely worn by a priest or a chieftain in a religious ceremony, maybe alongside sun-worship rituals, definitely not swung into a shield wall. That's over eighteen hundred years separating these horns from the first recorded Viking raid on Lindisfarne in 793. Would you mistake your great-great-great-grandparent's wedding china for something you use in a bar fight? That's roughly the gap we're talking about.

But 19th-century antiquarians didn't always draw that line carefully. Early collectors and popular illustrators, digging through old hoards without modern dating tools, lumped anything old and Nordic into one romantic bucket labeled ancient Norse warrior. A ceremonial priest's headdress from the Bronze Age and a Viking raider a thousand years later got flattened into the same imagined figure. That mistake didn't stay buried in a museum basement. It walked straight onto a stage.

In 1876, composer Richard Wagner's opera cycle Der Ring des Nibelungen premiered in Bayreuth, Germany. Costume designer Carl Emil Doepler dressed the Norse gods and warriors in flowing furs, winged helmets, and yes, dramatic curved horns. Wagner wanted mythic, larger-than-life figures towering over an audience from the back row of a theater. Historical accuracy wasn't the assignment. Spectacle was.

Why did that image spread so fast? Because it landed inside the Romantic movement, when artists across Europe were painting Norse myth as noble and untamed. Swedish painter Gustav Malmstrom and others had already sketched horned figures decades earlier, but Wagner's production put the look in front of thousands of paying theatergoers at once, night after night. A single stage costume became the visual template every illustrator copied afterward, because it was already proven to work on an audience.

From there it never stopped moving. By the early 1900s, horned helmets showed up on tourist postcards sold in Norway itself. In 1939, cartoonist Alex Raymond drew the horned warrior in his Flash Gordon comics. In 1948, the Minnesota Vikings didn't exist yet, but when the NFL team formed in 1961, they built their whole identity around that same horned image. Have you ever questioned why a football team from Minnesota wears Bronze Age Danish ceremonial gear? Most people never do.

But can we really say never, with total certainty? Here's the honest complication. Most Viking-age helmets we'd expect to find were probably never made of iron at all. Leather, boiled and hardened, wood, and antler don't survive well underground for a thousand years, especially in acidic Scandinavian soil. If a helmet had small horns made from antler lashed on with leather cord, that cord and antler could rot into nothing within a few centuries, leaving no rivet holes, no discoloration, no trace at all. So when archaeologists say no evidence, they mean no surviving evidence. Absence isn't automatically proof of absence. It just means if it happened, it happened in a material that time was never going to let us keep.

So go back to that charge down the hillside, the helmet with two long curved horns catching the firelight. That image didn't come from a Viking battlefield at all. It came from a Bronze Age priest's ritual, borrowed by a German opera designer in 1876, and sold to the entire world ever since. Wagner's costume department gave you a myth so good, so visually perfect, that even a total absence of battle evidence couldn't kill it.

Somewhere in a Norwegian museum, a plain iron dome with a simple eye guard sits under glass, unglamorous, undramatic, and true. Nobody buys a postcard of it. Nobody puts it on a football helmet. Real history is rarely as loud as the myth built on top of it. Next time you see those curving horns on a lunchbox or a mascot, you're not looking at Norse memory. You're looking at a nineteenth-century costume designer's best sales pitch, one that's still working on you today.

hero.reasoning: The narration is a myth-debunking explainer that does not follow a single named person through a throughline. Instead it places the viewer into a familiar imagined moment and repeatedly contrasts broad archetypes (Viking warrior, Bronze Age priest, theater costume designer, archaeologist). Visual continuity is therefore carried by stable role archetypes (including two viewer avatars for different eras), not a single heroic individual.

world.era: Mix of periods as needed: Viking Age (c.793–1066 CE), Nordic Bronze Age (c.1700–500 BCE) for ritual objects, 19th century for Romantic/theatrical scenes, and present day for museum and popular-culture contexts.
world.geography: Northern European (Scandinavia) implied by pine silhouette and rocky low hills in Viking scenes; flat peat bog landscape with reeds for Bronze Age scenes; urban stadium silhouette for modern mascot shots.
world.architecture: Minimal, episode-specific: Viking-era wooden longhouse silhouettes and timber longship outlines for background silhouette; Bronze Age ritual site shown as open wetland/bog with reed clumps and a shallow watery edge; 19th-century theater with proscenium arch suggested by a simple curved arch silhouette and heavy stage curtains (flat shapes); museums depicted as modern glass-and-stone display cases with labeled placards.
settingFamilies: Bronze Age ritual site / bog/hoard setting
Museum/gallery close-up display and modern postcard/mascot contexts
world.weatherTimeConventions: Dramatized Viking charge scenes: low warm firelight or sunset orange to increase drama. Bronze Age ritual scenes: soft neutral daylight. Theater scenes: spotlight (bright warm yellow rectangle on stage) with the rest of stage darker. Museum scenes: even cool gallery lighting.
world.environmentalColorRules: Historical/archaeological scenes use muted earth tones (dull greens, browns, grays) and desaturated blue-gray skies; myth/theater/mascot scenes use saturated accent colors (gold, bright red) to emphasize spectacle; museum galleries use neutral off-white walls and cool display-glass blue tints.
historicalScientificConstraints: No depiction of authenticated Viking-age helmets with attached horns (archaeological record lacks horned battle helmets).
Veksø bronze helmets are Bronze Age ceremonial objects and must be shown as thin decorative bronze, not robust iron battle gear.
Gjermundbu and other Viking-age helmets are iron rounded caps with nasal guards and must be represented as such when shown.
world.recurringEnvironmentConstruction: 3 flat layers per scene: background silhouette (sky/landmarks), midground (contextual props: ships, longhouse, stage arch, museum wall), foreground (characters and key objects). No texture; use thin black outlines and flat fills.

palette.contrastRules: Keep high-contrast accents (bronze-gold, spotlight-yellow, stadium-blue) limited to myth/theater/mascot objects; use low-contrast, desaturated colors for archaeological evidence. Ensure text/placard color contrasts with background (dark gray text on offwhite placards).
palette.environmentPaletteRules: Archaeological and Bronze Age scenes favor muted-forest-green, earth-brown, sandy-tan, and dull-iron-gray. Theatrical and mascot scenes add theater-red, spotlight-yellow, and bronze-gold as saturated accents. Museum interiors use museum-offwhite and cool blue tints for glass surfaces.

textPolicy.exceptionsPolicy: A short (<=5 word) exact phrase may be requested directly of the image model only when it is naturally part of the drawn artwork itself (e.g. a sign, a clock face) AND the configured renderer has demonstrated adequate text fidelity for this recipe — otherwise all text is composited as a deterministic overlay after the base image.

bible.visualTone: matter-of-fact and slightly wry: clear, evidence-first visuals that puncture grand myth with calm, almost deadpan comparisons; drama when showing the myth (stage lighting, exaggerated horns), restrained and neutral when showing archaeological reality (muted palettes, clinical framing).
negativeRules: painterly, sketchy, or textured drift away from flat solid fills
stickman construction mutating into a more detailed/realistic character mid-episode
shading, gradients, or texture appearing despite the flat-fill policy
Do not depict any authenticated Viking burial helmet as having horns.

Do not suggest that the presence of no horns in surviving iron helmets is definitive proof that horns never existed; instead, visually represent the preservation caveat (e.g., show a faint dashed-outline suggestion labeled 'possible perishable attachment — no surviving trace').
Do not mix theatrical horn designs into archaeological closeups or museum placards (the theatrical horn helmet must only appear in theater or modern-pop-culture contexts).

styleContract.detailLevel: Minimal — enough to read instantly at a glance, never busy or cluttered
styleContract.lineLanguage: Uniform thin, clean black outlines of identical weight everywhere; no sketchiness, no variable line weight, no cross-hatching
styleContract.realismLevel: Non-realistic, iconographic — identity is carried by a handful of discrete flat features, never facial realism
styleContract.colorStrategy: Use desaturated earth tones for 'real' historical material to communicate restraint and evidence; reserve saturated warm/gold and red for the myth/thespian stage and modern commercial images to emphasize spectacle and show how the dramatic image 'wins' visually.
styleContract.shadingPolicy: None — flat solid fills only, no gradients, no soft shadow rendering, no highlights
styleContract.shapeLanguage: Simple geometric primitives — circles, rounded rectangles, straight or gently curved lines — never intricate or organic detail
styleContract.dimensionality: 2D flat, no 3D rendering, no depth shading, no perspective distortion beyond simple flat-layer staging
styleContract.lightingStrategy: Simple flat lighting conventions: neutral even lighting for museum and archaeological close-ups; warm low-angle orange rim light for dramatized Viking charge to mimic firelight and create spectacle; single round warm spotlight for theater stage shots. No gradients or shading; lighting conveyed purely by flat color planes (warmer flat fill for spotlight, darker fill for background stage).
styleContract.illustrationStyle: Simplified stickman/doodle explainer construction — circle heads, dot eyes, stick limbs, mitten hands — never a detailed or semi-realistic character
styleContract.backgroundStrategy: 2-3 flat color layers (background/midground/foreground), never a fully rendered or photographic environment
forbiddenStyleTraits: realistic anatomy, fingers, or necks on stickman characters

bible.visualPremise: Flat 2D stickman explainer showing the contrast between an imagined, theatrical Viking (horned) and the sparse archaeological reality (plain iron helmets and ritual Bronze Age objects), switching between battlefield dramatization, museum close-ups, and 19th-century stage reconstructions.

cameraLanguage.framingConventions: Establishing wide shots for charges and theater stage; medium close-ups for helmet comparisons; tight close-ups (3/4 head) for placards and rivet detail on iron helmets; split-screen/side-by-side for myth vs reality comparisons.
cameraLanguage.visualHierarchyRules: When myth and reality are shown together, place the myth object slightly larger and more saturated to visually show why it dominates public imagination, but include a labeled, evenly scaled archaeological object on the opposite side to allow factual comparison.
cameraLanguage.simplicityReadabilityRules: Every frame must read clearly at thumbnail size — avoid busy multi-subject compositions unless the beat's own visual concept specifically requires comparing multiple subjects at once
cameraLanguage.whenEstablishingVsCloseupVsDiagram: Use establishing wide shot for the opening Viking charge; use closeups for Gjermundbu and Veksø helmets with placards; use diagram/timeline frames when explaining dates and preservation issues.

objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Used repeatedly as the episode's exemplar of authenticated Viking-age helmet construction (the key archaeological counterexample to horned images).
objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: Gjermundbu helmet (canonical illustration): plain rounded iron cap with a slightly flattened dome, dark iron flat-fill, and a prominent vertical nasal guard extending down the face's center; visible rivet heads at the rim only where the cap sections meet, no sockets or holes for horns, no cheek plates attached. Presented on a neutral museum pedestal with a small rectangular placard reading 'Gjermundbu helmet, c. 970 CE'.

objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Used whenever the episode explains the prehistoric source of horned headgear and to contrast ceremonial bronze horns with Viking-age iron helmets.
objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: Veksø bronze horned helmet (canonical illustration): very thin decorative bronze cap with two long gracefully curving horns rising symmetrically from the sides and tipped with small flat circular discs; bronze rendered as flat warm-gold color with thin black outline; overall delicate silhouette suggesting ceremonial use, not combat. Displayed on a low plinth with a placard reading 'Veksø helmets, Nordic Bronze Age, c. 1000 BCE'.

objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Represents the 19th-century theatrical moment that popularized horned imagery and is used to explain the diffusion of the myth into popular culture.
objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: Wagnerian theatrical horned helmet (canonical illustration): oversized stylized helmet with exaggerated glossy-gold curved horns (thicker base, sweeping upward), heavy theatrical fur trim around the base, and visible costume fastenings; designed for stage spectacle rather than practicality. Presented in a theater backstage rack or shown worn by the opera_costume_designer_archetype in a costume sketch.

objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Used to show the modern cultural spread and ubiquity of the horned-Viking image (tourist merchandise, sports branding, postcards).
objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: Museum postcard/mascot depiction (canonical illustration): flattened, high-contrast graphic of a horned Viking silhouette in bright saturated colors (e.g., crimson background, black silhouette with gold horns) framed like a postcard. For mascot: a rounded-corner stylized horned helmet logo with two oversized horns colored bright gold on a team-blue background. Include a small tag-line or label when used ('Souvenir postcard' or 'Vikings (mascot)').

objectLanguage.whyRecurring: Used in cutaways that explain preservation issues and excavation contexts (to show why organic materials might not survive).
objectLanguage.canonicalDescription: Excavation tray and trowel (canonical illustration): small rectangular artifact tray with soft padding and a single labeled artifact tag reading 'fragment' next to a tiny rusted iron fragment; trowel is a small flat triangular silhouette with a wooden handle. Colors: tray light gray, trowel handle brown, tool metal dark gray.

roleArchetypes.role: the viewer as a Viking-era raider (second-person avatar for 'you're charging' moments)
roleArchetypes.usedFor: All 'you' lines set in Viking-era scenes: the opening charge, dramatized raids, any scene inviting the viewer to imagine being a Viking.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Stickman viewer_viking: short stocky stickman body proportion, skin tone: fair-light neutral. Head: round stickman head with short straight dark-brown hair cropped around ears. Face: simple two-dot eyes and a neutral mouth (can be set to screaming/angry for charge scenes). Outfit: brown-tan wool tunic ending mid-thigh with a narrow stitched collar visible, gray-brown trousers, simple leather belt with round bronze buckle at the center front. Footwear: short brown leather boots. Accessories: round wooden shield (plain, radial planks visible as a single thin outline), short iron sword at belt (flat silhouette), small round bronze brooch at tunic shoulder (visible). Helmet: when used for realism scenes, a plain iron dome helmet with a single vertical nasal (nose) guard and no horn sockets; when used for myth scenes the same stickman may be shown wearing an exaggerated theatrical horned helmet but that horned helmet is an OBJECT and not part of the stickman canonical helmet description. Persistent identifying features (viewer_viking): short dark-brown hair; brown-tan wool tunic; round wooden shield; plain iron nasal helmet (when historically accurate). Forbidden mutations: hair must never be blond or long; tunic must never be patterned or modernized; helmet must never acquire riveted horn sockets in the canonical description.

roleArchetypes.role: the viewer in modern-day scenes (museum visitor, seeing postcards, modern consumer)
roleArchetypes.usedFor: All present-day lines: seeing postcards, mascots, football logos, museum visits, modern commentary.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Stickman viewer_modern: average modern adult stickman proportions, skin tone: fair-neutral. Head: short tidy black hair combed to the side. Face: two-dot eyes and neutral mouth (can smile or read expression). Outfit: plain short-sleeve teal T-shirt, dark denim-blue jeans, low-top gray sneakers. Accessories: small black backpack strap over one shoulder (suggesting museum visit), a modern camera/phone silhouette in one hand when shown photographing exhibits. Persistent identifying features (viewer_modern): teal T-shirt; black side-part hair; camera/phone accessory. Forbidden mutations: viewer_modern must never wear any anachronistic Viking or Bronze Age clothing unless playing a role in a dramatized scene that also includes the viewer_viking archetype.

roleArchetypes.role: generic Viking warrior used whenever the narration shows the mythic or the archaeological typical warrior
roleArchetypes.usedFor: Historical comparisons, cutaways to typical Viking raider scenes, and to demonstrate what real Viking-age equipment looks like.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Stickman viking_warrior_archetype: average adult male-tone stickman, skin tone: light-olive. Head: short tousled dark-brown hair and short beard (three-stroke beard under chin). Outfit: plain green wool tunic mid-thigh, gray chainmail suggested only by a thin outlined hem (no texture), dark trousers. Armor/helmet (historical): plain iron rounded cap with small vertical nasal guard and a short cheek-strap silhouette; NO horns, no elaborate crests. Weapon: one-handed round wooden shield (plain with a centered iron boss) and a short straight iron sword in a simple scabbard. Emotional expression language: aggressive/charging (open mouth) for dramatized myth shots; calm/neutral for archaeological/context shots. Persistent identifying features: rounded iron dome helmet with nasal guard; round wooden shield with iron boss; short dark-brown hair and short beard. Forbidden mutations: helmet must never show attached horns or rivet holes intended for horns in any historical/archaeological depiction.

roleArchetypes.role: representative Bronze Age ritual figure used when showing the Veksø and other ceremonial helmets
roleArchetypes.usedFor: Showing the prehistoric origin of horned headgear and making clear those horns predate the Viking Age by many centuries.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Stickman bronze_age_priest_archetype: slender stickman with pale-beige skin tone. Head: long straight blond hair to shoulders (simple single-shape hair fill). Outfit: long embroidered brown tunic with a decorative horizontal band across chest (band shown as a single darker-brown stripe). Accessories: thin bronze arm-ring on upper arm (single small oval), and the specific bronze ceremonial helmet (see objectLanguage entry for Veksø helmet) perched on the head. The bronze helmet appears as a thin bronze curved cap with two long upward-curving bronze horns, each horn tipped with a small flat disc; the helmet silhouette is delicate and slightly off-center on the head to suggest ceremonial placement rather than combat fit. Persistent identifying features: long blond hair; decorative chest band; the thin bronze horned helmet. Forbidden mutations: this archetype's helmet must never be drawn as robust iron suitable for combat; bronze must be visibly thin and decorative.

roleArchetypes.role: 19th-century theatrical costumer or stage figure used to show how horned imagery was popularized on stage
roleArchetypes.usedFor: All scenes that reference Wagner, 19th-century theater productions, costume design, and the moment the horned look was popularized on stage.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Stickman opera_costume_designer_archetype: middle-aged stickman with small monocle (single circle over right eye) and neatly trimmed dark hair with a small mustache. Outfit: high-collared black frock coat, white cravat visible at throat, and a pencil in the breast pocket. Accessories: holding a simple flat sketch sheet showing a stylized horned helmet silhouette (rough sketch lines), and optionally a pair of exaggerated theatrical horns (large, curved, stylized props colored bright gold). Persistent identifying features: monocle; black frock coat with white cravat; sketch sheet showing horned silhouette. Forbidden mutations: must not wear modern clothing or sports apparel.

roleArchetypes.role: modern archaeologist or museum curator who explains finds
roleArchetypes.usedFor: All explanatory cutaways: pointing to Gjermundbu helmet, discussing preservation issues, showing excavation scenes and museum labels.
roleArchetypes.canonicalAppearance: Stickman archaeologist_archetype: adult stickman with short salt-and-pepper hair, round glasses (thin frame), and a beige field jacket with two visible breast pockets and a small name badge on the right pocket. Accessories: clipboard or labeled artifact tray, small trowel silhouette when digging scenes, and when in the museum a labeled placard next to artifacts. Emotional expression language: calm, interested, explanatory. Persistent identifying features: beige field jacket; round glasses; clipboard or artifact tray. Forbidden mutations: must not wear theatrical costume or any anachronistic armor.

neverDrift: the recipe's own universal style (flat 2D, uniform outline, flat fills, no shading/gradients/texture)
Never show a Viking-age iron helmet with attached horns or horn sockets.
Never depict the Veksø helmet as robust iron combat gear; represent it as delicate bronze ceremonial headwear.
Viewer archetypes must remain visually consistent (viewer_viking distinct from viewer_modern).
allowedToVary: Viewer emotional expression (neutral, screaming, curious) as narrative context requires.
Scale of myth images can be exaggerated for rhetorical effect, but object design must respect material distinctions.
episodeWideConsistencyRules: Whenever horned helmets are shown as myth/theatrical they must use the 'wagner_theatrical_horn_helmet' or 'museum_postcard_and_mascot' canonical objects; archaeological frames must always use 'gjermundbu_helmet' or 'vekso_helmet' canonical objects.
Placards for archaeological objects must include approximate dates and brief labels (e.g., 'Gjermundbu helmet, c. 970 CE', 'Veksø helmets, Nordic Bronze Age, c. 1000 BCE').

graphicLanguage.colorUse: Uses this episode's own palette (muted-forest-green (#5B7A57), earth-brown (#8B5A2B), dull-iron-gray (#66696B), sandy-tan (#D4B48A), bronze-gold (#C19134)) as flat fills, consistent with narrative scenes — never a separate infographic color scheme.
graphicLanguage.lineStyle: The exact same line weight and fill language as narrative scenes — a graphic must never look like a different visual universe from the story frames around it
graphicLanguage.mapConventions: Small simplified map of Scandinavia (flat silhouette in muted-forest-green) used to place finds; sites marked with tiny dot and label in dark-gray text.
graphicLanguage.arrowsConnectors: Simple flat-filled arrow shapes and thin connector lines, same line language as everything else
graphicLanguage.comparisonLayouts: Two-column horizontal splits for direct comparisons: left column = myth/theatrical imagery (saturated), right column = archaeological reality (muted). Keep objects centered on each column with matching scale for immediate visual comparison.
graphicLanguage.backgroundBehavior: Clean, uncluttered flat backgrounds (often light/white or the episode's own environment palette) — never assumed to be white-only; the Production Bible's graphic language decides per episode
graphicLanguage.diagramConventions: Archaeological comparison diagrams use side-by-side flat silhouettes with a single thin black divider line and small rectangular placards beneath each object. Use arrows sparingly with thin black strokes and small caption boxes (museum-offwhite background).
graphicLanguage.whitespaceBehavior: Generous but not empty — whitespace isolates the one idea a graphic communicates, it is never filler
graphicLanguage.overlayTextBehavior: A short (<=5 word) exact phrase may be requested directly of the image model only when it is naturally part of the drawn artwork itself (e.g. a sign, a clock face) AND the configured renderer has demonstrated adequate text fidelity for this recipe — otherwise all text is composited as a deterministic overlay after the base image.
graphicLanguage.timelineConventions: Simple horizontal timeline with three labeled nodes: 'Nordic Bronze Age (c.1000 BCE)' at left with a small bronze helmet icon; 'Viking Age (c.793–1066 CE)' in center with Gjermundbu helmet icon; '19th century / modern' at right with a stage/mascot icon. Use muted baseline color and node accents in bronze-gold for the Bronze Age node and dull-iron-gray for the Viking node.
graphicLanguage.symbolicMetaphorLanguage: Use theatrical spotlight and stage curtain as recurring metaphors for 'myth as performance' and museum pedestals/placards as metaphors for 'evidence and labeling'.
graphicLanguage.characterUseInsideGraphics: Stickman characters, objects, and simplified environments are explicitly ALLOWED and encouraged inside a graphic when they clarify the point — a graphic is a composition family, never a text-only template

factualVisualConstraints: Do not invent rivet holes or attachment points on Gjermundbu or other Viking-age iron helmets that would imply horns were attached.
Show Veksø helmets as Bronze Age objects dated centuries before the Viking Age, never presented as contemporaneous Viking military equipment.

When showing archaeological excavation scenes, suggest that organic materials (leather, antler) may have decayed by showing empty soil with labeled 'no surviving organic attachment' rather than fabricating preserved leather straps.

cast.label: the viewer as a Viking-era raider (second-person avatar for 'you're charging' moments)
cast.description: Stickman viewer_viking: short stocky stickman body proportion, skin tone: fair-light neutral. Head: round stickman head with short straight dark-brown hair cropped around ears. Face: simple two-dot eyes and a neutral mouth (can be set to screaming/angry for charge scenes). Outfit: brown-tan wool tunic ending mid-thigh with a narrow stitched collar visible, gray-brown trousers, simple leather belt with round bronze buckle at the center front. Footwear: short brown leather boots. Accessories: round wooden shield (plain, radial planks visible as a single thin outline), short iron sword at belt (flat silhouette), small round bronze brooch at tunic shoulder (visible). Helmet: when used for realism scenes, a plain iron dome helmet with a single vertical nasal (nose) guard and no horn sockets; when used for myth scenes the same stickman may be shown wearing an exaggerated theatrical horned helmet but that horned helmet is an OBJECT and not part of the stickman canonical helmet description. Persistent identifying features (viewer_viking): short dark-brown hair; brown-tan wool tunic; round wooden shield; plain iron nasal helmet (when historically accurate). Forbidden mutations: hair must never be blond or long; tunic must never be patterned or modernized; helmet must never acquire riveted horn sockets in the canonical description.

cast.label: the viewer in modern-day scenes (museum visitor, seeing postcards, modern consumer)
cast.description: Stickman viewer_modern: average modern adult stickman proportions, skin tone: fair-neutral. Head: short tidy black hair combed to the side. Face: two-dot eyes and neutral mouth (can smile or read expression). Outfit: plain short-sleeve teal T-shirt, dark denim-blue jeans, low-top gray sneakers. Accessories: small black backpack strap over one shoulder (suggesting museum visit), a modern camera/phone silhouette in one hand when shown photographing exhibits. Persistent identifying features (viewer_modern): teal T-shirt; black side-part hair; camera/phone accessory. Forbidden mutations: viewer_modern must never wear any anachronistic Viking or Bronze Age clothing unless playing a role in a dramatized scene that also includes the viewer_viking archetype.

cast.label: generic Viking warrior used whenever the narration shows the mythic or the archaeological typical warrior
cast.description: Stickman viking_warrior_archetype: average adult male-tone stickman, skin tone: light-olive. Head: short tousled dark-brown hair and short beard (three-stroke beard under chin). Outfit: plain green wool tunic mid-thigh, gray chainmail suggested only by a thin outlined hem (no texture), dark trousers. Armor/helmet (historical): plain iron rounded cap with small vertical nasal guard and a short cheek-strap silhouette; NO horns, no elaborate crests. Weapon: one-handed round wooden shield (plain with a centered iron boss) and a short straight iron sword in a simple scabbard. Emotional expression language: aggressive/charging (open mouth) for dramatized myth shots; calm/neutral for archaeological/context shots. Persistent identifying features: rounded iron dome helmet with nasal guard; round wooden shield with iron boss; short dark-brown hair and short beard. Forbidden mutations: helmet must never show attached horns or rivet holes intended for horns in any historical/archaeological depiction.

cast.label: representative Bronze Age ritual figure used when showing the Veksø and other ceremonial helmets
cast.description: Stickman bronze_age_priest_archetype: slender stickman with pale-beige skin tone. Head: long straight blond hair to shoulders (simple single-shape hair fill). Outfit: long embroidered brown tunic with a decorative horizontal band across chest (band shown as a single darker-brown stripe). Accessories: thin bronze arm-ring on upper arm (single small oval), and the specific bronze ceremonial helmet (see objectLanguage entry for Veksø helmet) perched on the head. The bronze helmet appears as a thin bronze curved cap with two long upward-curving bronze horns, each horn tipped with a small flat disc; the helmet silhouette is delicate and slightly off-center on the head to suggest ceremonial placement rather than combat fit. Persistent identifying features: long blond hair; decorative chest band; the thin bronze horned helmet. Forbidden mutations: this archetype's helmet must never be drawn as robust iron suitable for combat; bronze must be visibly thin and decorative.

cast.label: 19th-century theatrical costumer or stage figure used to show how horned imagery was popularized on stage
cast.description: Stickman opera_costume_designer_archetype: middle-aged stickman with small monocle (single circle over right eye) and neatly trimmed dark hair with a small mustache. Outfit: high-collared black frock coat, white cravat visible at throat, and a pencil in the breast pocket. Accessories: holding a simple flat sketch sheet showing a stylized horned helmet silhouette (rough sketch lines), and optionally a pair of exaggerated theatrical horns (large, curved, stylized props colored bright gold). Persistent identifying features: monocle; black frock coat with white cravat; sketch sheet showing horned silhouette. Forbidden mutations: must not wear modern clothing or sports apparel.

cast.label: modern archaeologist or museum curator who explains finds
cast.description: Stickman archaeologist_archetype: adult stickman with short salt-and-pepper hair, round glasses (thin frame), and a beige field jacket with two visible breast pockets and a small name badge on the right pocket. Accessories: clipboard or labeled artifact tray, small trowel silhouette when digging scenes, and when in the museum a labeled placard next to artifacts. Emotional expression language: calm, interested, explanatory. Persistent identifying features: beige field jacket; round glasses; clipboard or artifact tray. Forbidden mutations: must not wear theatrical costume or any anachronistic armor.

props.label: Gjermundbu helmet (canonical illustration): plain rounded iron cap with a slightly flattened dome, dark iron flat-fill, and a prominent vertical nasal guard extending down the face's center; visible rivet heads at the rim only where the cap sections meet, no sockets or holes for horns, no cheek plates attached. Presented on a neutral museum pedestal with a small rectangular placard reading 'Gjermundbu helmet, c. 970 CE'.

Veksø bronze horned helmet (canonical illustration): very thin decorative bronze cap with two long gracefully curving horns rising symmetrically from the sides and tipped with small flat circular discs; bronze rendered as flat warm-gold color with thin black outline; overall delicate silhouette suggesting ceremonial use, not combat. Displayed on a low plinth with a placard reading 'Veksø helmets, Nordic Bronze Age, c. 1000 BCE'.

Wagnerian theatrical horned helmet (canonical illustration): oversized stylized helmet with exaggerated glossy-gold curved horns (thicker base, sweeping upward), heavy theatrical fur trim around the base, and visible costume fastenings; designed for stage spectacle rather than practicality. Presented in a theater backstage rack or shown worn by the opera_costume_designer_archetype in a costume sketch.

Museum postcard/mascot depiction (canonical illustration): flattened, high-contrast graphic of a horned Viking silhouette in bright saturated colors (e.g., crimson background, black silhouette with gold horns) framed like a postcard. For mascot: a rounded-corner stylized horned helmet logo with two oversized horns colored bright gold on a team-blue background. Include a small tag-line or label when used ('Souvenir postcard' or 'Vikings (mascot)').

Excavation tray and trowel (canonical illustration): small rectangular artifact tray with soft padding and a single labeled artifact tag reading 'fragment' next to a tiny rusted iron fragment; trowel is a small flat triangular silhouette with a wooden handle. Colors: tray light gray, trowel handle brown, tool metal dark gray.
